params.title: Marine
params.subtitle: VHF channels, SSB and SITOR, survival craft beacons, weather fax and NAVTEX, and NMEA data networks.

onScreen: VHF, SSB and SITOR, survival craft beacons, weather fax, NAVTEX and NMEA data
scenes.narration: Welcome to Marine, the lesson on the radio gear found aboard boats and ships. As a technician, you may be asked to install, check or repair this equipment, and the exam tests the channels, frequencies, modes and wiring rules behind it. We'll follow one boat as its radio installation grows. First comes a VHF, or very high frequency, radio for nearby contacts, then a single sideband radio for long distances. Next come the beacons packed in the life raft, then receivers for weather charts and safety messages, and finally the data network that links it all. No background is assumed. By the end, you'll know each exam answer, and why it's right.

params.title: Frequency: how fast a wave repeats
items: A radio wave swings back and forth, cycle after cycle
Frequency: cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz)
1 kilohertz (kHz) = 1000 Hz; 1 megahertz (MHz) = 1000 kHz
1 gigahertz (GHz) = 1000 MHz

onScreen: A radio wave repeats, cycle after cycle
Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
scenes.narration: Let's start with the idea every radio in this lesson depends on: frequency. Every radio signal is a wave of energy that swings back and forth, over and over, a little like a vibrating guitar string. One complete swing is called a cycle, and the number of cycles each second is the frequency, measured in hertz. Radio frequencies are huge numbers, so we use bigger units. A kilohertz is 1000 hertz. A megahertz is 1000 kilohertz. A gigahertz is 1000 megahertz. Each radio service is given its own frequencies, just as each station on a car radio has its own spot on the dial, so they don't talk over each other.

marks.label: VHF: about 156 MHz
marks.note: Marine VHF radio, reaches the horizon

scenes.narration: Those frequencies are grouped into bands, and this lesson visits several, so here's the map. Medium frequency, or MF, runs from 300 kilohertz to 3 megahertz; NAVTEX, a service sending safety messages to ships, works there at 518 kilohertz. High frequency, or HF, starts at 3 megahertz. MF waves hug the curve of the Earth, and HF waves bounce off the upper atmosphere, so both travel far beyond the horizon. That's why ships use them for long-distance radio. Marine VHF sits around 156 megahertz. Its waves travel in nearly straight lines, so they stop at about the horizon. Higher still, distress beacons use 406 megahertz, and ship radars work near 9 gigahertz. We'll visit each stop in turn.

marks.label: Channel 16: 156.800 MHz
marks.note: A channel number names one frequency

onScreen: Neighboring channels 25 kHz lower and higher
scenes.narration: Our first stop is marine VHF, the radio nearly every boat carries. You pick a VHF frequency by channel. So what is a channel? Think of the VHF band as a highway, and each channel as one lane. A channel number is simply a short name for one exact frequency: channel 16 is 156.800 megahertz. A radio signal isn't a thin line on the dial; it takes up some width, so lanes need space between them, or neighboring signals would overlap. Marine VHF channels, from 156 to 162 megahertz, use a channel spacing of 25 kilohertz: each channel sits 25 kilohertz from its neighbors. On the exam, pick 25 kilohertz; 10, 12.5 and 20 kilohertz are the wrong lane widths.

params.title: FM: the voice swings the frequency
labels: Carrier: a steady wave on the channel frequency
Your voice pushes its frequency up and down
Deviation: how far it swings from center
Marine VHF limit: ±5 kHz

onScreen: Carrier: steady wave on the channel frequency
Voice swings the frequency up and down
Deviation: the size of the swing
scenes.narration: To put your voice into its lane, a VHF radio uses FM, frequency modulation; modulation means changing a wave so it carries information. The radio makes a steady wave on the channel frequency, the carrier, which your voice rides on. As you speak, your voice nudges the carrier's frequency above and below center, in step with the sound. How far it swings is the deviation; a louder voice swings it farther. Too wide a swing would spill into the next lane. The maximum allowable deviation for VHF marine radios is plus or minus 5 kilohertz, meaning 5 kilohertz either side of center. Swings of 15 or 25 kilohertz would overrun the channel, and 2.5 kilohertz isn't the marine limit.

params.title: Does ±5 kHz fit a 25 kHz channel?
steps: f<sub>m</sub> = 3 kHz, the highest voice pitch

scenes.narration: Does a signal swinging plus or minus 5 kilohertz really fit in a 25 kilohertz lane? Check its bandwidth, the total width of the band the signal occupies. Carson's rule estimates it: bandwidth equals 2 times the sum of delta f and f sub m. Delta f is the deviation, 5 kilohertz. F sub m is the highest audio frequency, the highest pitch in the voice, about 3 kilohertz; the voice's own tones spread the signal a little beyond the swing. Add them: 8 kilohertz, the signal's reach on each side of center. Double it for both sides: 16 kilohertz. That's less than 25, so the signal fits, with room to spare as a guard between lanes.

params.title: Channel 16: distress and calling
items: Channel 16 = 156.800 MHz
Distress: a vessel in serious danger calling for help
Calling: make contact here, then move to a working channel
Not channel 70, 21A or 68

onScreen: Calling: first contact, then a working channel
scenes.narration: So every channel is a 25 kilohertz lane. Some lanes have special jobs, and 2 matter most on the exam. The first is channel 16, 156.800 megahertz. It's assigned for distress and calling. Distress means a vessel in serious danger calling for help. Calling means making first contact: you call another boat on channel 16, then you both switch to a working channel, an ordinary channel for conversation, so 16 stays clear. Because boats keep a listening watch on channel 16, it's like a town square where everyone can hear a shout for help. The trap answers, channels 70, 21A and 68, are not the distress and calling channel.

params.title: Channel 16 for voice, channel 70 for DSC

marks.label: Channel 70: 156.525 MHz
marks.note: DSC and acknowledgement only: no voice

onScreen: Channel 16, 156.800 MHz: distress and calling by voice
Channel 70, 156.525 MHz: DSC and acknowledgement only
scenes.narration: Channel 16 carries voice. Its partner, channel 70, carries data. Modern marine radios have DSC, digital selective calling. Instead of speaking, the radio sends a short burst of digital code, numbers sent as data the way a computer sends them. The code calls one particular station, a bit like dialing a phone number, and makes the other radio ring. A distress button sends an automatic alert the same way, carrying the boat's identity. Channel 70, 156.525 megahertz, is used for DSC and acknowledgement only: the calls, and the replies confirming they arrived. Voice is never allowed on channel 70, because talking there would block the digital alerts. So: 16 for distress and calling by voice, 70 for DSC.

params.title: Simplex versus duplex
rows: Both at once, like a phone

onScreen: Duplex: 2 frequencies, both talk at once
Duplex: calls through a coast station
scenes.narration: Marine VHF radios also have a switch the exam asks about, the USA-INT control. To understand it, you need 2 words: simplex and duplex. A simplex channel uses one frequency for both directions. You talk, then you let go of the button and listen, taking turns like a walkie-talkie; most boat-to-boat talk works this way. A duplex channel uses 2 frequencies, one for each direction. The ship transmits on one, and the coast station, a radio station on shore, transmits on the other, so both can talk at once, like a telephone. The international marine channel plan makes some channels duplex, often for calls through coast stations. But in U.S. waters, several of those channels are used differently.

callouts.label: USA: some normally duplex channels become simplex
USA mode: those channels send and receive on the ship frequency
INT: restores international duplex operation
Neither setting increases range

onScreen: USA: some duplex channels become simplex
Sends and receives on the ship frequency
scenes.narration: That's where the USA-INT control comes in; the name is short for USA and international. In U.S. waters, some channels that are normally duplex channels are used as simplex channels. The USA setting changes them into simplex: for those channels, the radio transmits and receives on the ship frequency, the one the ship normally transmits on. The INT setting restores international duplex operation, for use in other countries' waters. Notice what the control doesn't do. It doesn't turn simplex channels into duplex; that's backwards. And setting INT doesn't increase range. Range depends on transmitter power and antenna height, and the switch changes neither.

params.title: Checking the GPS feed to a DSC radio

callouts.label: GPS receiver: works out the boat's position from satellites
Position sent to the radio as data sentences
Check: latitude and longitude, plus speed, on the display

onScreen: GPS works out the boat's position
Look for latitude, longitude and speed on the display
scenes.narration: One last VHF check, done on every DSC installation. A distress alert is far more useful when it says where the boat is, so installers connect a Global Positioning System receiver, or GPS, to the DSC radio. It uses signals from satellites to work out the boat's position. The GPS receiver sends that position over a data cable as short lines of text called sentences; more on that cable later in the lesson. So how might an installer verify the correct GPS sentence is reaching the radio? Look for latitude and longitude, the boat's position on the map, plus speed, on the VHF display. If they appear and look right, the data is arriving.

params.title: Never test with the distress button
items: Never press and hold the red distress button to test
It sends a false distress alert, and rescuers respond
No separate GPS confirmation readout: the position is the proof
Another station's radio check can't see your GPS data

onScreen: Never test with the red distress button
It sends a false distress alert
The position on the display is the proof
A radio check can't see your GPS data
scenes.narration: What you must never do is press and hold the red distress button to test the link. That sends an actual DSC distress alert: a false alarm that rescuers must treat as genuine, tying up the people who answer real emergencies. The exam's other traps miss the point too. There's no separate GPS confirmation readout to look for; the position on the display is the proof. And asking another station for a radio check won't help, because it can't see what your GPS sends your radio. That wraps up VHF: 25 kilohertz channels, plus or minus 5 kilohertz deviation, channel 16 for distress and calling by voice, and channel 70 for DSC.

params.title: AM: a carrier and 2 sidebands
labels: Carrier: steady, holds none of the voice
Lower and upper sidebands: the voice, mirrored

onScreen: Carrier in the middle: no voice
scenes.narration: But VHF reaches only about as far as the horizon, and offshore our boat needs long range, so we add an MF and HF radio. Its voice mode is single sideband, or SSB. To understand it, start with plain AM, amplitude modulation. Amplitude is the strength of the wave, and in AM your voice changes that strength. This picture shows the signal by frequency, not time: low on the left, high on the right, with the steady carrier in the middle. Changing its strength with your voice creates new frequencies on either side: a band just below the carrier and a band just above, called sidebands. The voice lives entirely in those sidebands, 2 mirror images carrying the same speech.

params.title: SSB: one sideband, no carrier
labels: Carrier removed
One sideband removed
All the power goes into the voice
No speech, no output

onScreen: All the power in the voice
scenes.narration: Single sideband trims away the waste. The carrier carries no information, so SSB removes it. The 2 sidebands carry the same speech, so SSB drops one of them too. What's left is a single sideband, which takes less room on the band and puts all the transmitter's power into your voice. There's a consequence the exam cares about. With no carrier, an SSB transmitter puts out nothing while you're silent. Its output rises and falls with your speech, syllable by syllable, and so does the power it draws.

params.title: Powering the SSB radio: a circuit

onScreen: Red positive lead: current flows out
Black negative lead: current flows back
scenes.narration: Where does that power come from? The boat's batteries. Think of water in a pipe. Voltage is the battery's push, like water pressure, and current is the flow that push drives. Current leaves the battery's positive terminal along the red lead, and comes home to its negative terminal along the black lead. In between, it flows through the radio and powers it. It has to make that whole loop, called a circuit, to flow at all; break the loop anywhere, and the flow stops. An ammeter, a meter that measures current, shows how much the radio is drawing.

params.title: Voice-testing an SSB aboard a boat
labels: Each syllable: a surge of output and current
The ammeter swings up with each word, not down
Voltage panel indicator lamps may glow with each syllable
Battery voltage dips with each surge: a voltage drop

onScreen: A current surge with each syllable
Panel lamps may glow with each syllable
Battery voltage dips with each surge
scenes.narration: Now picture voice-testing the SSB aboard a boat. Each syllable you speak makes a burst of output, and with it a surge of current from the battery. Between words, the current falls back. So the ammeter swings up with each word, because speaking increases the current; it doesn't fluctuate down. Those surges, plus stray radio energy picked up by the boat's wiring, cause a common occurrence: the voltage panel indicator lamps, the little lights on the boat's electrical panel, may glow with each syllable. Each surge also pulls the battery's voltage down a little. That loss of push is called a voltage drop. So the trap answer, minimal voltage drop at the power source, is wrong.

params.title: From the radio to the tuner
items: Transceiver: a transmitter and receiver in one box
Coax: a center wire inside a braided metal shield
Automatic tuner: matches the antenna to each frequency
Once matched, it holds: no retuning on each syllable

onScreen: Transceiver: transmitter and receiver in one box
Coax: center wire inside a braided shield
It holds its setting while you talk
scenes.narration: Next, follow the radio's output toward the antenna. The SSB radio is a transceiver, a transmitter and receiver in one box. Its signal leaves on coax, a cable with a center wire inside a braided metal shield. The coax runs to an automatic antenna tuner. An antenna works best at certain frequencies, but an SSB radio uses many. So the tuner adjusts itself to match the antenna to each frequency you use, letting the power flow into the antenna instead of bouncing back toward the radio. Once matched, it holds that setting while you talk, so it doesn't cycle on each syllable: that's another trap answer for the voice test.

blocks.label: Automatic antenna tuner
blocks.note: Matches the antenna to each frequency

blocks.label: Insulated backstay
blocks.note: Mast-bracing wire used as the antenna

onScreen: RF ground: connection to the seawater
scenes.narration: Here's the whole antenna system. The transceiver feeds the tuner through coax. From the tuner, one wire runs to the antenna. On a sailboat, the antenna is often the backstay, the wire that braces the mast toward the stern, the back of the boat. Insulators at each end separate it electrically from the mast and hull, so it can serve as the antenna. The tuner's other connection goes to an RF, or radio frequency, ground: a connection to the seawater, which acts as the other half of the antenna.

callouts.label: Automatic antenna tuner
Tuner to backstay: very high RF voltage
GTO-15 high-voltage cable: tuner to the insulated backstay
Coax such as RG-8U or RG-213: transceiver to tuner

onScreen: Very high RF voltage from tuner to backstay
GTO-15 high-voltage cable: tuner to backstay
RG-8U or RG-213 coax: transceiver to tuner
scenes.narration: Which wire connects the tuner to the insulated backstay? Where the tuner feeds the end of a long wire like a backstay, the radio energy appears as very high RF voltage, enough to spark through ordinary insulation. So that run uses GTO-15 high-voltage cable: a single wire with very thick insulation, the kind made for neon signs. Coax, such as RG-8U or RG-213, belongs between the transceiver and the tuner, where the voltage is modest and the shield keeps the signal inside the cable. On the exam, RG-8U and RG-213 are traps for the backstay run, and so is ordinary 16-gauge two-conductor wire.

params.title: Fuses and resistance
items: Fuse: a thin metal link that melts if too much current flows
One fuse in the red lead, one in the black lead
Resistance: anything that holds the current back
More resistance, more voltage drop under a heavy load

onScreen: Fuse melts if too much current flows
A fuse in the red lead and in the black lead
scenes.narration: That's the antenna side. Back on the power side, the exam asks about a fault, and it takes 2 more ideas to follow. First, fuses. A fuse is a thin metal link that melts and opens the circuit if too much current flows, protecting the wiring from overheating. The SSB has one in the red lead and one in the black lead. Second, resistance: anything that holds the current back, like a narrow section of pipe. Pushing current through resistance uses up some voltage, which is where a voltage drop comes from. The more resistance, and the heavier the load, meaning the current being drawn, the bigger the drop.

callouts.label: Blown black negative fuse
Return current takes another path: coax shield, tuner, RF ground
More resistance: the voltage drops under transmit load
Blown red positive fuse: the radio simply shuts off

onScreen: Return current via coax shield, tuner, RF ground
Blown red fuse: radio shuts off
scenes.narration: Here's the fault, and it ties the power side to the antenna side. Your marine SSB shows apparent low voltage when transmitting. A likely cause is a blown black negative fuse. The current still has to get back to the battery, so it finds another path, such as the coax shield, the tuner and the RF ground. That path has more resistance, so under the heavy transmit load the voltage drops. A blown red positive fuse is different: no current can reach the radio, so it simply shuts off. The other traps don't fit either. Good grounding helps rather than hurts, and an antenna mismatch affects the signal going out, not the supply voltage.

params.title: SITOR: typed messages by radio
items: SITOR: simplex teletype over radio
Teletype: each typed character sent as a short code
HF fading and static can wipe out characters
2 cures: ask for a repeat, or send everything twice

onScreen: Each character sent as a short code
Fading and static wipe out characters
Cures: ask for a repeat, or send twice
scenes.narration: The SSB radio can carry text as well as voice. Ships send typed messages over MF and HF using SITOR, simplex teletype over radio. Teletype means each typed character is sent as a short code, a pattern of 2 kinds of signal, much like dots and dashes, and printed at the far end. Simplex, as with VHF, means one frequency, taking turns. The challenge is that HF signals fade, and bursts of static can wipe out characters. SITOR has 2 cures. The receiver can check the text and ask for a repeat of anything damaged. Or the sender can transmit everything twice, so a spare copy is always on the way.

params.title: ARQ: send 3 characters, wait for an answer

blocks.label: Sender: next block, or a repeat

onScreen: Receiver answers at once: OK or repeat
Then the next block, or a repeat
scenes.narration: The first cure is ARQ, automatic repeat request, a two-way exchange between 2 stations. The sending station transmits the message in data groups of 3-character blocks. After every block, it pauses. The receiving station checks the block and acknowledges it right away, replying either OK or please repeat. Then the next block goes. It's like reading a phone number to someone 3 digits at a time, waiting for them to say got it. So on the exam, ARQ transmissions are not acknowledged only at the end of the message; every block is answered. ARQ is also called SITOR-A.

params.title: FEC: every character sent twice
labels: Each character is sent twice, at different moments
A noise burst wipes out one copy
The receiver prints the good copy, without replying
One-way, not interactive; time diversity is FEC's, not ARQ's

onScreen: Receiver prints the good copy, no reply
scenes.narration: The second cure, FEC, forward error correction, takes the other approach. The sender transmits each character twice, with time diversity: the 2 copies go out at different moments, like saying everything twice on a bad phone line. If a burst of noise wipes out one copy, the other usually survives, and the receiver prints the good one. The receiver never replies. That makes FEC one-way, not interactive, so on the exam, forward error correction is not an interactive mode. Notice which mode uses time diversity: FEC. ARQ doesn't rely on time diversity, and ARQ doesn't send each character twice; it repeats a block only when asked. FEC is also called SITOR-B.

blocks.label: Coast radio station
blocks.note: Weather and safety broadcasts in FEC

onScreen: Why weather and safety broadcasts use FEC
scenes.narration: Because FEC needs no reply, any number of ships can copy the same transmission at once. Two-way communication with the coast radio station using FEC is not necessary to be able to receive the broadcasts. There's no link to set up, and no answerbacks to exchange; those are the identity codes stations swap at the start of an ARQ contact. That's exactly why weather and safety broadcasts use FEC. One trap claims that sending every character twice would make weather broadcasts too long; in fact, FEC is the mode they use.

onScreen: SFEC: one-way to a single station
scenes.narration: There's one more mode: SFEC, selective FEC. It works like FEC, but the message is addressed to a single station instead of everyone. Now line all 3 up, because the exam gives them as a sequence. ARQ is two-way communication. FEC is one-way communication to all stations. SFEC is one-way communication to a single station. So the sequence ARQ, FEC, SFEC means two-way, one-way to all stations, one-way to a single station. The takeaway for SSB and SITOR: with no carrier, current surges with speech; high-voltage cable feeds the backstay; ARQ answers every block; FEC sends twice and needs no reply.

params.title: When the crew takes to the survival craft

onScreen: EPIRB alert relayed by satellites to a rescue center
Rescue ship's radar finds the SART
Handheld VHF for talking to rescuers nearby
scenes.narration: Now the worst case: the crew must abandon ship and take to a survival craft, a life raft or lifeboat. GMDSS, the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System, is the international set of rules and equipment that makes sure they're found. 3 radio tools go with them. An EPIRB, emergency position-indicating radio beacon, sends a distress alert to satellites, which relay it to a rescue center. A SART, search and rescue radar transponder, guides the rescue ship in on its radar. And a handheld VHF lets survivors talk to rescuers nearby. We'll start with the SART, which needs a quick look at radar.

params.title: Radar: echoes at a bearing and range
labels: Pulses out, echoes back: a later echo means a farther object
Own ship at the center; each echo at its bearing and range
Ship radars: X-band near 9 GHz, S-band near 3 GHz

onScreen: Own ship at the center; echoes at their bearing and range
Ship radars: X-band near 9 GHz, S-band near 3 GHz
scenes.narration: Here's radar in a nutshell. It sends out short pulses of microwaves, radio waves in the gigahertz range, from a spinning antenna. When a pulse hits a ship or a coastline, an echo bounces back, like a shout echoing off a cliff. The radar times each echo: the longer it takes to return, the farther away the object. The round display puts your own ship at the center and draws each echo as a bright spot, in the direction it came from, called its bearing, and at its distance, called its range. Ship radars use 2 bands: X-band, near 9 gigahertz, and S-band, near 3 gigahertz. Keep that 9 in mind.

params.title: The SART: silent until a radar asks

callouts.label: Activated in the survival craft: waits silently in standby
A radar pulse interrogates it
Only then does it transmit its reply

scenes.narration: Now the SART itself. A transponder is a device that transmits a reply when it receives a signal, and the SART is one. After being activated in the survival craft, it waits silently in standby. It begins transmitting only when it responds to radar interrogation: a pulse from a searching ship's radar asks, and the SART answers. That saves its battery, and nobody needs to operate it. So the exam's trap answers are wrong. A SART doesn't begin radiating immediately when activated, manual or water activation alone doesn't make it radiate, and the operator never keys it.

params.title: Which band does a SART answer?

marks.label: 406 MHz
marks.note: The EPIRB's frequency, not the SART's

scenes.narration: Which radar can wake a SART? A search and rescue transponder operates in the 9 gigahertz band, roughly 9.2 to 9.5 gigahertz, so it answers X-band radars. It does not operate at 3 gigahertz: it only listens in the 9 gigahertz band, so an S-band radar won't trigger it. And it does not operate at 406 megahertz; that frequency belongs to the EPIRB, as we'll see shortly. On the exam, choose 9 gigahertz, and treat 3 gigahertz, S-band and 406 megahertz as traps.

params.title: Why a SART makes dots
labels: The SART sweeps through the 9 GHz radar band
12 sweeps in each reply
Each pass through the radar's frequency: a burst it hears
Later bursts are drawn farther out: a line of dots

onScreen: SART sweeps through the 9 GHz band
Each pass: a burst the radar hears
scenes.narration: When it answers, the SART doesn't reply on one frequency. It sweeps through the whole 9 gigahertz radar band, 12 times. The searching radar listens on just one frequency. Each time the sweep passes through that frequency, the radar hears a short burst. Remember that radar turns time into distance: a burst that arrives later is drawn farther out. So 12 bursts, arriving one after another, are drawn as 12 spots in a line.

params.title: A SART on the radar display
labels: Ordinary echoes: other ships and land
SART: 12 equally spaced dots outward along its bearing
Within about a mile: the dots become arcs, then circles

onScreen: SART: 12 equally spaced dots along its bearing
Within about a mile: arcs, then circles
scenes.narration: Here's what the rescuers see. Among the ordinary echoes, the SART signal appears as a series of 12 equally spaced dots, extending outward from the SART along its bearing. A line of dots like that stands out from anything else on the screen. As the ship closes within about a mile, the dots spread into arcs, and then into complete circles. That's because up close the SART's reply is so strong that the radar hears it even while its antenna points a little away, so the dots smear sideways. Circles tell the crew they're very close. On the exam, the answer is 12 equally spaced dots; dashes, 20 dashes and spirals are traps.

params.title: EPIRB on 406 MHz: the primary locating signal

blocks.label: Satellites
blocks.note: Hear the burst, find its position

onScreen: Alert relayed to a rescue center
Primary GMDSS locating signal: EPIRB on 406 MHz
scenes.narration: The SART helps with the final approach, but first rescuers must learn there's an emergency, and where. That's the EPIRB's job. Once activated, either by hand or automatically when it floats free of a sinking ship, it transmits on 406 megahertz. Satellites pick up the signal, work out where the beacon is, and relay the alert to a rescue center. So under GMDSS, the primary source of transmitting locating signals is an EPIRB transmitting on 406 megahertz. The trap is a SART transmitting on 406 megahertz; SARTs work at 9 gigahertz. A radio direction finder only measures a direction, and a survival craft transceiver is for talking, so neither is the answer.

callouts.label: A digital data burst, not a voice channel
Unique hexadecimal identification number
Hexadecimal: digits 0 to 9, then letters A to F
Registered to one vessel and its emergency contacts

onScreen: Hexadecimal: 0 to 9, then A to F
scenes.narration: What does the EPIRB actually send? Not speech. A 406 megahertz EPIRB transmits a digital data burst, a short packet of code, repeated again and again. Inside is a unique hexadecimal identification number. Hexadecimal is a way of writing numbers with 16 symbols, the digits 0 to 9 followed by the letters A to F, so the ID looks like a string of 15 numbers and letters. The owner registers each ID in a national database, along with the vessel's details and emergency contacts, so rescuers can look up whose beacon is calling. On the exam, the trap says it allows immediate voice communications with the rescue center; it doesn't.

params.title: What the EPIRB signal tells rescuers

callouts.label: Identifies the vessel
Used to determine the position of the beacon
Does not describe the nature of the distress
Not the vessel's name and port: a coded ID that rescuers look up

onScreen: Used to find the beacon's position
Not the nature of the distress
A coded ID, not name and port
scenes.narration: So once activated, a satellite EPIRB transmits a signal used for 2 things: identifying the vessel, through that registered ID, and determining the position of the beacon. The satellites can work out the position from the signal itself. As a satellite passes, the beacon's frequency seems to rise and then fall, like the pitch of a passing siren, and that pattern shows where the beacon is. Or the beacon includes GPS data in its burst. What the code does not do is describe the nature of the distress: it can't say fire, flooding or sinking. Nor does it spell out the vessel's name and port of registry; it carries the coded ID, which rescuers look up.

params.title: The 2 beacons side by side
rows: Raises the alarm, locates from afar
Hexadecimal ID in a data burst

onScreen: EPIRB heard by satellites, SART by radar
EPIRB alerts and locates, SART guides in
scenes.narration: Before we leave the life raft, set the 2 beacons side by side, because the exam's traps love to swap them. The EPIRB works on 406 megahertz; the SART works in the 9 gigahertz radar band. The EPIRB is heard by satellites; the SART answers a searching ship's radar. So the EPIRB raises the alarm and locates the survivors from afar, and the SART guides the rescuer in close. And the EPIRB sends a hexadecimal ID in a data burst, while the SART shows up as 12 dots on the radar display. That's the takeaway for survival craft.

params.title: Weather fax: charts by radio
items: Facsimile: printed pictures sent for permanent display on paper
The classic marine example: weather charts
The picture is scanned and sent line by line
HF shore stations, 3 to 23 MHz: 120 lines per minute

onScreen: Facsimile: printed pictures for permanent display on paper
Scanned and sent line by line
HF weather fax: 120 lines per minute
scenes.narration: Back aboard, the crew wants forecasts, so we add receivers for shore broadcasts, starting with weather fax. Facsimile, or fax, is the transmission of printed pictures for permanent display on paper, such as weather charts. The station scans the chart one thin line at a time. The receiver prints each line as it arrives, building the picture strip by strip. So fax isn't television, and it isn't typed characters forming a picture. Sender and receiver must keep the same pace, or the chart comes out slanted. For HF weather fax from shore stations, 3 to 23 megahertz, the standard scan rate is 120 lines per minute. 240 lines per minute, and 150 or 60 lines per second, are traps.

params.title: How the shades travel: FSK
labels: Frequency-shift keying: the shade sets the frequency
Grays fall between black and white
Black and white: 800 Hz apart
The center frequency ± 400 Hz

onScreen: Frequency-shift keying: shade sets the frequency
scenes.narration: How does a shade of gray travel by radio? Weather fax uses frequency-shift keying, or FSK; keying just means switching. The signal shifts its frequency according to the shade being scanned: one frequency means white, another means black, and grays fall in between. For HF weather fax, black and white are 800 hertz apart: the center frequency plus or minus 400 hertz. So the whole signal lives in a slice of the band less than 1 kilohertz wide. That slice is what the receiver must let through.

params.title: Band-pass filters and decibels
items: Band-pass filter: passes one slice of frequencies, blocks the rest
Crystal lattice: quartz crystals give sharp, steep edges
Decibels (dB): a scale for comparing signal strengths
-6 dB: the signal cut to about half its voltage

scenes.narration: To let through just that slice, the receiver uses a filter, because it hears a whole crowd of signals and noise. A band-pass filter lets through one slice of frequencies and blocks everything outside it, like a doorway only so wide. The best ones use a crystal lattice, a network of quartz crystals. Each crystal vibrates at one exact frequency, like a tuning fork, which gives the filter sharp, steep edges. A filter's width is measured between the points where it has weakened the signal by a set amount, given in decibels, a scale for comparing signal strengths. Minus 6 decibels means the signal is cut to about half its voltage.

params.title: The fax filter: 1 kHz wide at -6 dB

marks.label: 6 kHz
marks.note: Too wide: lets in needless noise

scenes.narration: So which width suits weather fax? The signal spans 800 hertz. A good crystal lattice band-pass filter for HF weather fax has a bandwidth of 1 kilohertz at minus 6 decibels: wide enough to pass the whole frequency-shift keying signal, with a little margin, while rejecting noise and neighboring stations. The trap widths fail. 500 hertz is narrower than the 800 hertz shift, so it would clip the tones. 6 kilohertz and 15 kilohertz would pass the signal, but they also let in far more noise than needed. The takeaway for weather fax: 120 lines per minute, and a 1 kilohertz filter.

marks.label: 2182 kHz
marks.note: SSB voice: NAVTEX isn't received here

marks.label: 4209.5 kHz
marks.note: Some HF NAVTEX, but not the primary

onScreen: 518 kHz: used exclusively for NAVTEX internationally
scenes.narration: The second receiver is for NAVTEX, short for navigational telex: an automated service that broadcasts safety messages to ships as text. Coast stations around the world take turns on one frequency: 518 kilohertz is the primary frequency used exclusively for NAVTEX broadcasts internationally. Watch its neighbors on the exam. NAVTEX is not received on 2182 kilohertz using SSB; that's a voice frequency. 2187.5 kilohertz is a DSC distress frequency, for digital alerts. And 4209.5 kilohertz carries some NAVTEX on HF, but it isn't the primary international one.

callouts.label: Receives MSI broadcasts in SITOR-B, or FEC, mode
Ships only receive: they never transmit on 518 kHz
No ARQ: it needs two-way handshaking
Messages printed or shown here

onScreen: MSI in SITOR-B or FEC mode
scenes.narration: What does NAVTEX carry? MSI, maritime safety information: navigational warnings, weather warnings and search and rescue notices. It's sent with SITOR, which we met in the SSB section. NAVTEX receives MSI broadcasts using SITOR-B, which is FEC mode: each character sent twice, with no reply needed. That fits, because one coast station is talking to every ship in range at once. Ships only receive; they never transmit, so the trap saying the ship station transmits on 518 kilohertz is wrong. And ARQ, SITOR-A, isn't used, because it needs two-way handshaking, a reply for every block, which a broadcast can't have. A small dedicated receiver prints the messages or shows them on a screen, with no one needing to tune in.

params.title: Choosing what NAVTEX prints
items: Each message header: station letter, subject indicator, serial number
Subject indicator: the kind of message
Subject programmed for rejection: the message is not printed
Never rejected: navigational and meteorological warnings, search and rescue messages

onScreen: Header: station, subject indicator, serial number
Navigational, meteorological and search and rescue messages can't be rejected
scenes.narration: Can the crew choose what gets printed? Partly. Every NAVTEX message starts with a short header: a letter for the transmitting station, a letter called the subject indicator, which says what kind of message it is, and a serial number. The operator can program the receiver to reject chosen subjects. Then it does not print a message whose subject indicator matches one programmed for rejection. But navigational warnings, meteorological, or weather, warnings and search and rescue messages cannot be rejected; they're too important to miss. The traps fail because the receiver only reads the header. It can't judge whether a message concerns your vessel, and the station letter picks stations, not subjects. NAVTEX in short: 518 kilohertz, FEC, receive only.

onScreen: GPS position shared with other devices
scenes.narration: Our boat's electronics now need to share information. The GPS position feeds the DSC radio, as we saw earlier, and also the chart plotter, an electronic map, and the autopilot, which steers. For devices from different makers to understand each other, they follow standards from NMEA, the National Marine Electronics Association. 2 standards are on the exam: the older NMEA 0183 and the newer NMEA 2000. They wire things together in very different ways, so let's take them one at a time.

onScreen: Serial link: bits one after another
scenes.narration: NMEA 0183 is a one-talker, multiple-listener serial link. Serial means the data travels as a stream of bits, the 1s and 0s of digital data, one after another along a single pair of wires. One device, the talker, sends; here it's the GPS, sending its position as those short text sentences. Several devices, the listeners, can receive on the same pair. But the data flows one way only: a listener can't talk back on that line. If the radio needs to send something, it needs a separate line of its own, as a talker.

onScreen: Shield terminated to ground at the talker
Both ends grounded: a noisy ground loop
scenes.narration: One NMEA 0183 wiring rule is on the exam. The data wires run inside a shield, a braided or foil wrapper that catches electrical noise and drains it away to ground, the boat's common electrical connection. How should the shield be grounded? Terminated, meaning connected, to ground at the talker, and unterminated, left unconnected, at the listener. Why only one end? 2 ground points on a boat are rarely at exactly the same voltage. Connect the shield at both ends, and a small current circulates through it between them. That's a ground loop, and it injects noise into the data line. Leaving both ends unconnected wouldn't drain the noise at all, and grounding only the listener is backwards.

Now the newer standard. NMEA 2000 is a true network. Every device connects to one shared cable, and any device can both send and receive. So NMEA 2000 is the bi-directional, multi-transmitter, multi-receiver network data language. Think of 0183 as a lecture, with one speaker and an audience, and 2000 as a group conversation, where anyone can speak and everyone hears. On the exam, the answer is NMEA 2000. NMEA 0183 is the one-talker link, and 0181 and 0182 aren't the network either.

params.title: NMEA 2000: one device fails, the rest carry on

blocks.label: Continuous backbone
blocks.note: Each device on a tee and drop cable

onScreen: Each device on a tee and drop cable
No interruption to all other devices
scenes.narration: How is that shared cable laid out? A main cable, the backbone, runs through the boat. At each device, a T-shaped connector called a tee sits in the backbone, and a short drop cable runs from it to the device. Like houses tapped off a water main, the devices hang off the backbone; it never runs through them. So if one device fails, like this depth sounder, which measures water depth, there will be no interruption to all other devices. The traps of the system shutting down, or of everything after the failed device going dead, imagine a chain, with each device passing signals along. And a device that simply stops working won't open the backbone's main fuse.

params.title: Power on the backbone: the LEN
items: The NMEA 2000 cable carries 12 volt power as well as data
Each device draws its current from the backbone
1 milliamp (mA) = 1 thousandth of an amp
Load equivalence number: LEN 1 = 50 mA

onScreen: Backbone carries 12 volt power and data
scenes.narration: The NMEA 2000 cable carries more than data. It also carries 12 volt power from the boat's battery, so devices can draw current right from it. Every device adds to the load, and the installer adds them up to size the power supply and cable. Current is measured in amps, and small currents in milliamps: a milliamp is a thousandth of an amp, so 1000 milliamps make 1 amp. To make the adding easy, each NMEA 2000 device has a load equivalence number, or LEN, which states its current in whole-number units. In an NMEA 2000 device, a LEN of 1 is equivalent to 50 milliamps of current consumption. Remember 50; 5, 10 and 25 milliamps are the traps.

params.title: Working out a LEN
steps: Not a whole number? Round up

onScreen: Round up if not a whole number
scenes.narration: Let's work one out. Each LEN stands for 50 milliamps, so a device's LEN is its current draw divided by 50 milliamps. Our device draws 300 milliamps. 300 milliamps divided by 50 milliamps is 6; the milliamps cancel, leaving a plain number. If the result weren't a whole number, you'd round up, so the plan never underestimates the load. Here it's exactly 6, so the LEN is 6. Does that make sense? 6 steps of 50 milliamps is 300 milliamps, so yes.

onScreen: Each tee: a device draws current
Limit: 1.5 volts at the end of the last segment
scenes.narration: Adding up the load matters because of voltage drop. Every cable has a little resistance, so current flowing through it loses some voltage along the way. That's the voltage drop we met with the SSB, and it works like water pressure falling along a long garden hose. The more current, and the longer the cable, the bigger the drop, so the last device on the backbone gets the lowest voltage. NMEA 2000 cabling plans set a limit: a voltage drop of 1.5 volts at the end of the last segment satisfies the plan. That keeps every device working even when the battery runs low. 0.5, 2.0 and 3.0 volts are the traps.

params.title: Where to feed the power in
items: Devices in a single location: an end-powered network
Power fed in at one end of the backbone
Short cable run from supply to loads: a small voltage drop
Devices spread along a long backbone: feed power mid-way

onScreen: Power fed in at one end
scenes.narration: So where should the power be fed in? It depends on where the devices are. An NMEA 2000 system with its devices in a single location, say all at the helm, the steering position, may be powered as an end-powered network, with power fed in at one end of the backbone. With the devices close together, the cable run between the supply and the loads stays short, and so does the voltage drop. When devices are spread along a long backbone, power is fed in mid-way instead, so the current divides both ways. Dual mid-powering is the trap for a single location. Powering devices individually misses the point: the backbone powers them, and NMEA 2000 devices do need 12 volts.

params.title: Key facts: Marine
items: VHF: 25 kHz channels, ±5 kHz deviation; 16 distress and calling; 70 DSC only
SSB: no carrier, surges with speech; GTO-15 to the backstay; ARQ two-way, FEC one-way
SART: answers 9 GHz radars with 12 dots; EPIRB: 406 MHz, hexadecimal ID
Weather fax: 120 lines per minute, 1 kHz filter; NAVTEX: 518 kHz, FEC, receive only
NMEA 0183: shield grounded at the talker; NMEA 2000: backbone, LEN 1 = 50 mA, 1.5 V drop

onScreen: SSB and SITOR: surges, GTO-15, ARQ and FEC
Fax 120 lines per minute; NAVTEX 518 kHz
NMEA: talker-end shield, backbone, 50 mA, 1.5 V
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up. On VHF, channels are 25 kilohertz apart, deviation is plus or minus 5 kilohertz, 16 is for distress and calling, and 70 for DSC only. On SSB, there's no carrier, so current surges with speech; GTO-15 cable feeds the backstay. SITOR's ARQ is two-way, FEC one-way. In the life raft, the SART answers 9 gigahertz radars with 12 dots, and the 406 megahertz EPIRB sends a hexadecimal ID. Weather fax runs at 120 lines per minute through a 1 kilohertz filter, and NAVTEX is on 518 kilohertz in FEC, receive only. NMEA 0183 grounds its shield at the talker, while on NMEA 2000, a LEN of 1 is 50 milliamps, with at most a 1.5 volt drop.
